transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?

Well, thank you, doctor. Honestly, what brings me in is just... I feel like I'm constantly running on a motor lately. It's like, I'm a special education teacher, and you know how demanding that can be, but it's more than just the job. It's like I finish one thing at school, say, getting the kids through a math module, and I immediately jump into the next thing, like organizing the sensory bins, without even taking a breath. And then I get home, and it's the same thing. I can't just sit down. I'm fixing a cabinet door, then I'm out pulling weeds in the garden before the glue even dries, and then I'm back inside trying to meal prep for the week. I just... I never seem to be able to shut myself off. My wife says it's exhausting just watching me, and to be honest, I'm exhausted too, but my brain or my body—I don't even know which—just won't let me stop moving. It's like this constant, buzzing need to be doing something, anything, every single second of the day.
Did you feel this same need to be constantly on the move when you were a child?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It's funny you ask that because, well, my mother—bless her heart, she really had her hands full with me—she used to always make this joke about me. We'd be at family gatherings, Thanksgiving or whatever, and she’d tell everyone that even back in elementary school, I was basically the one teaching the class from my seat. 

Because I was just... I was never actually *in* the chair. I’d be up, walking around the rows of desks, checking on what everyone else was doing, or I'd be talking. Always, always talking. And if the teacher was up at the front giving directions for an assignment, I couldn't even wait for her to finish her sentence. I’d just cut right in and start blurting things out or asking questions before she even got to the end of what we were supposed to do. As a special ed teacher myself now, I know exactly how disruptive that can be, but back then, I just... I couldn't hold it in. The words just fell out of my mouth. 

So, yeah, this constant motor, it’s been part of who I am long, long before adulthood. It’s definitely not something that just started up recently with this family change we've been dealing with. It’s like it’s been baked into me since I was a little boy, just constantly buzzing around the classroom. I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins, she actually used to try and give me these little jobs just to keep me from pacing, but even then I'd rush through them just so I could get back to... well, to doing whatever else popped into my head. But yes, to answer your question, it's always been exactly like this.
Along with feeling constantly on the go, do you also struggle with things like sustaining your attention, making careless mistakes, or losing track of details?

No, not really. I mean, it's funny you ask that, because my wife, she actually brought that up the other day. She was reading some article online, you know how it is, everyone's a doctor on the internet these days. And she asked me the exact same thing! She said, "Honey, do you think you have trouble focusing?" And I had to really sit down and think about it—well, not sit down, obviously, I was probably pacing around the kitchen island while she was talking—but I thought about it, and honestly, no. 

I don't lose things. In fact, I'm the one who finds everything in our house. If my wife loses her keys, I know exactly where they are. They're on the little hook by the garage door, or they're in the pocket of her blue coat. I remember details like that perfectly. And at work, I mean, you have to be detail-oriented to be a special education teacher. The paperwork alone is a mountain. You have IEPs, you have progress reports, you have data tracking for behavior plans... if I was making careless mistakes, I'd be in serious trouble, and my kids wouldn't get the services they need. 

So, no, I don't struggle with that end of things. When I'm working on a student's file, I am laser-focused. I can sit there—well, stand at my standing desk, really—and just power through it without missing a beat. It's just the physical part, the constant need to be moving, the blurting things out, the feeling like I'm driven by a motor... that's the part that's wearing me out. But as far as attention and details go, my mind is sharp as a tack. I just wish my body would let my mind take a rest every once in a while, you know?

These symptoms have been present since early elementary school and manifest across multiple environments (home, school, workplace).
